About: Twin Paradox — One-Way Signal

Source

Lecture
12 — Time dilation & the twin paradox
Simulation
One-way call / signal (no-return variant)
Concept
A moving twin's proper time runs slow — no turnaround needed; a light signal reveals the asymmetry cleanly.
Serves
Reading Minkowski diagrams · proper time along a worldline · light-cone invariance · Lorentz frame change.
Inquiry
What time does Alice's clock read when Bella's call arrives, and how does that compare to Bella's clock at emission?
Misconception
“Both twins age the same because motion is relative.” The one-way variant shows time dilation is real even without a turnaround.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A call from a receding ship

Here’s our setup. Alice stays on Earth at x = 0. Bella leaves the same event E₁ at constant speed and never turns back.

Somewhere along her worldline, at event EC, Bella reads her own clock and sends that reading home as a light pulse. Both worldlines are straight: nobody accelerates anywhere in this scene. Keep that in mind as we go.

2 · Bella's clock at the call

Let’s start with the call itself. Bella recedes at v = 0.60. In Alice’s frame she calls at tC = 5.00. What do you think Bella’s own clock reads at that event?

τB is live now — you can read it beside EC and in Clock readings.

3 · When the call lands

Now follow the call home. The pulse leaves EC at x = 3.00 and runs back to Alice at 45° — light speed, in every frame. What do you think Alice’s clock reads at the reception event ER?

τA is live now, and ER sits at ct = 8.00 on Alice’s worldline.

4 · Seeing versus ageing

Here’s where it gets interesting. A call reporting 4.00 lands when Alice’s clock reads 8.00 — a factor of 2.00. But in Alice’s frame, by what factor do you think Bella’s clock actually runs slow?

Try raising v/c: γ and the ratio τA/τB pull apart further.

5 · Bella's point of view

Now let’s be fair to Bella. She has the same right to call herself at rest; in her frame S′ it’s Alice who recedes at −v. Described in S′, whose clock do you think runs slow?

Switch the Frame to S′ and watch: ER moves to ct′ = 10.00 while τA holds at 8.00.

6 · What a one-way call settles

Let’s step back and see what we’ve learned. The boost to S′ moves every coordinate — EC to ct′ = 4.00, ER to ct′ = 10.00 — yet both clock readings survive it: 4.00 at the call, 8.00 at reception. A proper time, after all, is what a carried clock records.

The steady factor between them, k = √((1+v)/(1−v)) = 2.00, depends only on v. And since nobody accelerates and the twins never meet again, nothing here crowns a younger twin — for that, you need a turnaround.

The Physics

Twin paradox, one-way call · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Bella flies away from Alice at constant speed and never turns back. At one moment she reads her clock and calls home on a pulse of light, and the sim compares that reading with Alice's clock when the call arrives. It separates three things that are easy to run together: how a moving clock runs, how long light takes to cross the gap, and what each frame says about the other's clock.

What you'll learn

  • How a clock's reading depends on the worldline it follows through spacetime.
  • How to work out what Alice's clock reads when the call arrives.
  • How the ratio of the two readings is related to the Lorentz factor γ.
  • What changes when the same events are described from Bella's frame, S′.
A sketch of the diagram: Alice's worldline (cyan), Bella's (amber), and the call as a 45° light pulse from EC to ER.

What's on screen

  • Alice (cyan): at rest at x = 0, so her worldline is vertical.
  • Bella (amber): leaves E₁ at speed v. A dot climbs her line as the animation runs.
  • Light pulse (dashed): the call, a 45° ray from EC to Alice. The faint dashed cross is the light cone of E₁.
  • Event badges E₁, EC, ER: (x, ct) coordinates, plus a clock reading τ at EC and ER.
  • Events and Clock readings panels: the coordinates in the active frame, then γ, τB, τA and τA/τB.
See itSend the call at the opening settings (v = 0.60, tC = 5.0). Watch for: the amber dot climbing Bella's line, then the dashed pulse running from EC back to Alice's line.

Fixed: c = 1, so x and ct share one scale and light always runs at 45°. Bella moves at constant velocity and never turns back.

03

Proper time is the length of a worldline

A clock counts the proper time along its own worldline. Take c = 1, so ct and t are the same number. Alice sits at x = 0, so her clock reads the coordinate time Δt. Bella's clock reads

Proper time along a straight worldline at speed v.
  • Between E₁ and EC, Alice's frame measures Δct = tC and Δx = v tC. In Δs² = −(Δct)² + Δx² the spatial part has the opposite sign to the time part, so it shrinks −Δs², and with it Δτ = √(−Δs²).
  • So for the same Δct, a tilted worldline records less proper time than a vertical one. Nothing is wrong with Bella's clock: it is reporting its own path.
Bella's leg at the opening settings. The teal curve is every event 4.00 of proper time from E₁.

As in the lectures, the interval is Δs² = −(cΔt)² + (Δx)², negative for timelike pairs, and the proper time is Δτ = √(−Δs²)/c.

See itKeep tC fixed and change the lean of Bella's line. Watch for: τB changing while tC stays put. The closer her line leans to the 45° ray, the further τB falls below tC.
04

Light needs time to bring the call home

Bella sends the call at EC, at x = v tC. Light covers one unit of x per unit of ct in every frame, so the call is a 45° line in S and in S′. Its interval is zero:

The call is a null interval, the same in S and S′.

Alice is at rest in S, so her clock reading at ER is the coordinate time of ER: when the call left, plus the time light needs to cross the gap.

Alice's clock at the moment the call arrives.
Key idea. With c = 1, the call arrives later than it left by exactly the x-distance it has to cover. The faster Bella recedes, the bigger that gap.
See itSend a call at v = 0.80, tC = 4.0. Watch for: the pulse crossing the gap from EC to Alice's line at 45°, so ER sits above EC by as much as EC sits to the right of Alice.
05

What Alice sees is not how fast Bella ages

Compare the two readings the call joins: τA at reception and τB at emission. Their ratio is the factor k.

k is the Doppler factor. It depends on v only.
  • Time dilation, γ, is only one factor in k. The other, 1 + v, is the growing light-travel delay.
  • If Bella sent a call every 1.00 of her own time, Alice would receive them every k of hers, because each call starts from further away.
  • So the ratio of the two readings is how the call looks. γ is how fast Bella's clock runs.
v/c tC

See itCompare γ with τA/τB at v = 0.30 and then v = 0.90. Watch for: τA/τB staying above γ, and the gap between them widening as v grows.
06

Each frame finds the other's clock slow

In S′, Bella is at rest and Alice recedes at −v. The boost gives the coordinates of every event there:

The boost the Frame buttons apply.

It changes where the events sit, not what a clock reads at an event: τB and τA are the same in S and S′. What differs is which events each frame calls simultaneous.

Opening settings, drawn in S. Each frame's "now" through EC meets Alice's worldline at a different event.
  • In S, Alice reads 5.00 when Bella reads 4.00. Bella's clock is slow.
  • In S′, Alice reads 3.20 when Bella reads 4.00. Alice's clock is slow, by the same γ.
  • The two "now" lines meet two different Alice events, so both statements hold. The twins never meet again, so the sim cannot name a younger one. A reunion needs a turnaround.
See itSwitch to Bella's frame, S′. Watch for: ER in the card showing S′ coordinates, with τB and τA keeping the values they had in S.
07

Where it matters

  • Cosmic-ray muons. A muon's mean life of 2.2 μs would carry it about 660 m. At γ ≈ 22 its mean decay length in the ground frame is roughly 15 km, so many muons made 15 km up still reach sea level.
  • GPS. A satellite's speed alone makes its clock run about 7 μs a day slow. Gravity pulls the other way and wins, and the clocks are pre-adjusted. Without the corrections, position errors would grow by kilometres a day.
  • Doppler shifts. Light from a source receding along the line of sight arrives stretched by k = √((1+v)/(1−v)), the same k as the call, and spectroscopy of receding sources uses it.
Go deeper: why a round trip does settle it
  • Between two fixed events, the straight worldline has the most proper time. A twin who turns around follows a bent worldline between the same two events, so she records less.
  • The turnaround does not cause the difference. It is what lets the twins meet again, so their readings can be compared at one event.
08

Summary

In one line. A clock reads the proper time of its own worldline, and the call carries that reading across a gap that light needs time to cross. The ratio of the two readings is the Doppler factor k, not the dilation factor γ.

Key points

  • τB = tC/γ: the proper time of Bella's tilted worldline is less than tC.
  • τA = tC(1 + v): the time of emission plus the light-travel time.
  • τA/τB = k = γ(1 + v) = √((1+v)/(1−v)). It depends on v only, not on tC.
  • A boost moves coordinates, not clock readings. A one-way call names no younger twin.

Common mix-ups

  • "The ratio of the two readings is the time dilation factor." It is k = γ(1 + v). The dilation is γ alone, and the factor 1 + v is the light-travel delay.
  • "Each frame says the other's clock is slow, so one of them must be wrong." They compare different pairs of events, so both hold.
  • "Switching to S′ changes the clock readings." Only the coordinates move. τB and τA read the same.

Things to try on your own

  • Set v = 0.95 and tC = 9, then check in Clock readings that τA/τB equals γ(1 + v).
  • Drag EC along Bella's line and note which readings change and which do not.
  • Set v = 0.05. Compare how far τB sits below tC with how far τA sits above it.
